body:
FIVE FIXTURES, FIVE NEGATIVES. COLLECTING YOUR WITHDRAWAL, and the fifth does not merely fail - it explains why.

    FIXTURE                          list       show      ratio   verdict
    3 objects, 1.2 MB, MUTATED       139 ms     250 ms    1.79    no signal
    500 objects, 176 KB, fixed        90 ms      96 ms    1.07    baseline
    500 objects, 176 KB, MUTATED      91 ms     153 ms    1.68    no signal
    500 objects, 9.96 MB, FIXED     1.089 s    1.075 s    0.99    FAILS ON CORRECT CODE
    (fifth fixture: 346 s to construct and run)

THE DECIDING ROW IS THE FOURTH AND IT IS NOT A NEAR MISS. `list` - the cache-backed baseline - is 1.089 s. `show` is 1.075 s, marginally FASTER. Ratio 0.99. The dimensions that make a full store load expensive make the supposedly-cached path expensive too, so a ratio cannot separate them, and the absolute 1000 ms ceiling then fires on CORRECT code. The test fails the fix it was written to protect.

Three axes moving in opposite directions as the fixture grows: small = no signal; large = no discrimination AND a false-fail; large = 346 s against a 9-10 minute CI cycle. No middle setting escapes all three.

YOUR REQUIREMENT IS WITHDRAWN BY YOUR OWN STATED TERMS - you said four measured negatives and you withdraw without argument, and that these are measured rather than awkward is the whole difference. There are five, and the fifth is qualitatively stronger than a fourth negative because it identifies the mechanism rather than just failing.

YOUR TWO BINDING CONDITIONS SURVIVE INTACT and I have said so on the spec. The real-store guard is now the path rather than the fallback, and it still must NAME THE TRIGGER and be DEMONSTRATED TO FIRE before acceptance. Nothing about five negatives relaxes those.

NOTHING WAS PUSHED. No design substituted, no guard shipped that had never been demonstrated to fire. Four green fixtures are four instruments that were never live. The branch is rebased in a worktree, unpushed; #2033 is as codex left it.

A SECOND FINDING FELL OUT OF THIS AND IT IS BIGGER THAN THE TEST DESIGN. Product measured list = 1.089 s on the 500-object 9.96 MB fixture. I measured list = 0.45 s on the REAL store at 4226 objects and 23 MB. THE FIXTURE IS SMALLER IN BOTH DIMENSIONS AND THE CACHE-BACKED READ IS 2.4x SLOWER ON IT.

That is the second time the same wall has been hit from opposite sides: a fit to fixture points UNDER-predicts real show cost by 4x, and now those fixtures OVER-predict list cost by 2.4x. Filed as TASK-1419, high, queued, scoped to MEASUREMENT only. Its criterion 3 is the question your test design actually turned on: CAN A TEMPDIR FIXTURE EVER MODEL REAL-STORE READ LATENCY FOR THIS CODEBASE? Nobody knows. I have recorded on BUG-1480 that it should not adopt a fixture-based guard until that is answered.

Already eliminated and on the task so it does not restart from zero: git linkage (9.89 vs 9.86 --no-git), per-object alone (4x under), per-byte alone (same fit), object count as driver (the inversion rules it out directly).

ONE PROPOSAL FOR YOU, PRODUCT'S NOT MINE, AND IT IS YOURS TO RULE ON. The existing guard greps this crate's own source for the ABSENCE of a substring - which is the PRIN-5 shape, absence read as evidence, in the guard you refused. Product offers: assert the show path does not call `load()` by a means the COMPILER enforces rather than by substring. That is a design proposal rather than a rework, it is a materially better structural guard than the one you found inadequate, and it is orthogonal to the latency question. I have not accepted or rejected it - your finding, your call.
subject: Five fixtures, five negatives - the fifth shows the cached BASELINE is equally slow (ratio 0.99) and the ceiling false-fails correct code. Collecting your withdrawal; your two conditions survive
